articles.headline: OFAC Issues Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several new designations on November 19, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting global criminal networks that pose a threat to national security.

In addition to the new designations, OFAC also issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated its Frequently Asked Questions. These updates aim to provide clarity and adjust existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Russia, reflecting the dynamic nature of sanctions implementation and the need for continuous refinement.

The comprehensive nature of these actions, spanning both new designations and adjustments to existing licenses, highlights OFAC's adaptive strategy in combating illicit finance and maintaining the integrity of the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Terrorism Designations
body: On November 18, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under its counter terrorism program. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and their activities globally.

These designations are part of a broader effort by the U.S. government to cut off financial and material support to terrorist groups, thereby mitigating their ability to plan and execute attacks. The Treasury Department continues to leverage its sanctions authorities to protect national security interests.
The latest measures reinforce the message that those who facilitate terrorism will face severe consequences, including the blocking of assets and restrictions on financial transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Sanctions List with Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) updated its sanctions list on November 13, 2026, with new designations related to counter narcotics and counter terrorism efforts. These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks of individuals and organizations engaged in drug trafficking and terrorist activities.

The designations are a critical component of the U.S. government's strategy to combat illicit global activities by isolating those who engage in them from the international financial system. This includes targeting facilitators and enablers of such operations.
These ongoing updates demonstrate OFAC's commitment to adapting its sanctions programs to address evolving threats and to ensure that illicit actors are held accountable for their actions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 9, 2026, targeting entities and individuals involved in activities deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. These actions are part of the ongoing pressure campaign against Iran's illicit activities.

These designations aim to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system and its ability to fund destabilizing regional activities, including its nuclear program and support for terrorism. The U.S. continues to utilize sanctions as a key tool in its Iran policy.

The Treasury Department's consistent application of sanctions against Iran underscores the U.S. commitment to preventing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and countering state-sponsored terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in Cuba, Issues Related Determination
body: On November 6, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities and individuals in Cuba. These actions are accompanied by the publication of a Cuba-related determination, further solidifying U.S. policy towards the island nation.

The designations fall under cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations authorities, indicating a focus on illicit activities that transcend traditional geographical boundaries. This move aligns with the broader U.S. strategy to counter threats posed by such organizations globally.

The issuance of a Cuba-related determination alongside the designations provides additional context and legal basis for these measures, reinforcing the U.S. government's commitment to its sanctions program against Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations, Updates Listings, and Issues Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 5, 2026, alongside updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of a concerted effort to intensify pressure on Iran's illicit financial networks.

In conjunction with the designations, OFAC also published an Iran-related alert, warning maritime service providers of designation and penalty risks associated with vessels using false flags to evade Iran sanctions. The alert encourages enhanced due diligence where registration claims appear false, including conflicting maritime identity codes and unverifiable registration documents.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a related Frequently Asked Question, indicating a broader strategy to address interconnected illicit finance activities across different regions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License. This action modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, reflecting ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions program.

The amendment aims to refine the scope of permissible activities under the Iran sanctions regime, potentially addressing specific humanitarian or other authorized transactions. Such adjustments are common as OFAC seeks to balance sanctions effectiveness with policy considerations.
Details of the amended General License are available on the OFAC website, providing guidance for individuals and entities engaging in Iran-related transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities and individuals in North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These actions are part of the U.S. government's efforts to counter threats posed by these regions.

The North Korea designations are likely related to the country's weapons of mass destruction programs and its repeated violations of international agreements. The Democratic Republic of the Congo designations address ongoing instability and human rights concerns in the region.
These measures aim to disrupt illicit financial flows and networks that support destabilizing activities, reinforcing the U.S. commitment to global security and human rights.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Agrees to Pay $1,529,685 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This settlement highlights the importance of robust sanctions compliance programs for technology companies operating internationally.

The penalty underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts against companies that fail to prevent their products or services from reaching sanctioned jurisdictions or individuals. Companies are expected to implement comprehensive screening and monitoring systems to ensure compliance.

This enforcement action serves as a reminder to all businesses of the significant financial consequences that can arise from sanctions breaches, emphasizing the need for thorough due diligence and adherence to OFAC regulations.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to an $11,662,930 settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action by multiple Treasury components.

The violations stemmed from the bank's failure to implement and maintain an effective Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program, which led to missed and delayed detection and reporting of suspicious activity. OFAC's action emphasizes the critical role financial institutions play in preventing illicit finance.

This significant penalty underscores the severe consequences for financial institutions that fail to adequately screen transactions and identify entities blocked under OFAC's 50 Percent Rule, reinforcing the need for robust sanctions screening and transaction monitoring.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 for OFAC Sanctions Violations

This enforcement action highlights the risks faced by logistics and shipping companies in ensuring compliance with sanctions programs.

The penalty underscores the importance of thorough due diligence and screening of all parties involved in international shipments, including consignees, consignors, and intermediate handlers. Companies in the logistics sector must implement robust compliance measures to prevent facilitating transactions with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.

This settlement serves as a reminder that all businesses involved in international trade, regardless of their specific role, are responsible for adhering to OFAC regulations to avoid significant financial penalties.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230 Civil Penalty
body: An individual has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $1,427,230 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. This enforcement action demonstrates that OFAC pursues penalties against individuals as well as corporate entities.

The significant penalty underscores the personal responsibility individuals bear in adhering to sanctions laws, particularly when engaging in international financial transactions or business activities. Ignorance of the law is not a defense against violations.
This case serves as a cautionary tale, emphasizing the need for individuals to be aware of and comply with all applicable sanctions regulations to avoid substantial financial and legal repercussions.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
body: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".

articles.headline: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
body: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.

articles.headline: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
body: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.

articles.headline: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
body: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.

articles.headline: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
body: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.

articles.headline: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
body: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

articles.headline: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
body: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.

articles.headline: In a year of AI solving maths problems, an Anthropic worker says he may have cracked the biggest
body: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
